entry.title: Get an Email When Your EC2 CPU Spikes: CloudWatch + SNS
entry.summary:
High CPU on a server often goes unnoticed until users complain. Here is the fastest way to get an email the moment it happens, tested end to end on a real instance. The flow: EC2 → CloudWatch alarm → SNS topic → your inbox An AWS account and an email address you can open One region for everything (I used US East, N. Virginia) Choose Amazon Linux and the t3.micro instance type. Give it any name. Select the instance, then go to Actions > Monitor and troubleshoot > Manage CloudWatch alarms. Create a new SNS topic and use these settings:
Setting Value
Statistic Average
Metric CPU utilization
Alarm when
>= 40%
Period 5 minutes, 1 consecutive
Open SNS > Topics, select your topic and click Create subscription. Choose Email, enter your address, then click Confirm subscription in the email AWS sends you. Important: no confirmation means no alerts. Connect to the instance and generate CPU load: sudo su yum install stress -y stress --cpu 9 --timeout 600
The --timeout 600 stops the test after 10 minutes. You can also press Ctrl+C. CPU rose to about 50.9%. A few minutes later, this email arrived: State change: OK → ALARM Reason: a datapoint of about 50.94 was greater than or equal to the 40% threshold Link: straight to the alarm in the console That is exactly the early warning I wanted. Tip: 40% is for a demo. In production, use 70 to 80% over several periods to avoid noisy alerts. Stop stress, delete the alarm, delete the SNS topic and subscription, then terminate the instance. Full slides with screenshots and results: https://lnkd.in/p/dfxFhxMv https://www.linkedin.com/in/vishalpatil-devops-aws/ https://dev.to/vishal_patil_aws https://github.com/VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS

entry.title: How to Check a Pitch Shift Without Confusing It with Faster Playback
entry.summary:
If a recording sounds higher after editing, did its pitch change, or did the whole recording simply play faster? A small test can separate those two possibilities: inspect both frequency and duration. I'm Alex, part of the Creatune team. On October 17, 2026, I tested our public Pitch Changer with a locally created 440 Hz sine wave. This is a narrow functional check, not a listening-quality benchmark for vocals or full songs. In equal temperament, a shift of n semitones has frequency ratio: ratio = 2 ** (n / 12) expected_hz = input_hz * ratio
For 440 Hz and +12 semitones, the expected frequency is 880 Hz. A duration-preserving pitch shift should keep an 8-second input approximately 8 seconds long. Simple double-speed playback would also produce 880 Hz, but its duration would be about 4 sec…

entry.title: Fact lists beat inspiration when publishing must not slip
entry.summary: Missed publishing weeks rarely start with “we forgot English.” They start with an empty fact list: no dates, no deliverables, no approved boundaries—so the writer pads, and platforms punish the padding. A practical habit is a monthly checklist the operator can fill in twenty minutes: what shipped, what changed, what must not be claimed. Inspiration can wait; facts cannot. Some public pages describe write–design–post capacity to accounts you authorize. Useful only if the facts keep arriving. Packaging never promises rankings or citations. Boundary: don’t invent case studies; don’t stack CTAs; don’t same-title repost to hit a quota. Guanji Notes. Fill the list first—then write.

entry.title: I built a native Windows terminal workspace for repeatable dev workflows
entry.summary: MRE stands for Myeong-Ryeong-Eeda (명령이다), Korean for “It is a command.” The name sounds decisive; you still choose what to run. I built MREShell to bring the terminals, projects, and commands I use every day into one Windows app. It hosts the shells you already use, including PowerShell, Command Prompt, WSL, and Git Bash. You can organize terminals into workspaces, save reusable commands with parameters, and connect repeatable steps in runbooks. For example, save git switch {{branch}} once, then reuse it by choosing the branch when you need it. MREShell is free for personal and commercial use. It is a native Windows 11 x64 app and requires the Microsoft Visual C++ x64 Redistributable. Preview status: Version 1.2.0 Preview 1 is unsigned, and clean Windows 11 VM validation is still pending. Please review the release notes before trying it. Download MREShell.exe Release notes Report an issue or share feedback I’d especially appreciate feedback on the workspace setup and reusable command workflow. Where did you get stuck, or what would make this more useful in your daily work?

entry.title: Why a 1 TB Drive Shows Up as 931 GB (and Other Unit Traps)
entry.summary: You buy a 1 TB hard drive, plug it in, and your computer says 931 GB. It's not faulty and you haven't been cheated. It's one of several everyday unit traps that catch people out. Here are the most common ones and how to avoid them. Drive makers count in decimal: 1 TB is 1,000,000,000,000 bytes. Many operating systems count in binary, where 1 "GB" really means 1 gibibyte, or 1,073,741,824 bytes. Divide the drive's bytes by the binary figure and you get about 931. Same drive, two ways of counting. The fix is simply to know which one you're looking at. The binary units have their own names (KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB), and when you see those, you know the larger divisor is in use. A US gallon is about 3.785 litres. An imperial gallon is about 4.546 litres.
